research_text:
## API and finding

`javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec` is an `AlgorithmParameterSpec` that holds an initialization vector (IV). It does not itself encrypt data or generate an IV. Its constructors copy either an entire byte array or a selected range; `getIV()` returns a new array. The selected IV must also meet the requirements of the cipher and mode that use it. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html

**The particular event or value behind this finding is unknown.** The supplied report gives `UnsatisfiedConstraint` but no detector message or location. The rule contains several numeric constraints and a separate randomness predicate; the label alone does not identify which requirement or value the analyzer reported. CogniCrypt’s documentation distinguishes constraint errors from required-predicate errors, but does not establish the meaning of this particular label. ([eclipse.dev](https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/codeanalysis/?utm_source=openai))  
Source: https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/codeanalysis/

## The published CrySL rule

The source’s matching declaration is, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec

OBJECTS
	byte[] iv;
	int offset;
	int len;

EVENTS
	c1: IvParameterSpec(iv);
	c2: IvParameterSpec(iv, offset, len);
	Con := c1 | c2;

ORDER
	Con
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl

- The declared class is `javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec`; the events are constructor-shaped `IvParameterSpec` calls. Constructors have a constructed type rather than an ordinary method receiver.
- The event declarations **do constrain the parameter lists**: `c1` has one declared `byte[]` parameter; `c2` has that parameter followed by two declared `int` parameters.
- The rule declares `length[iv] >= offset + len`, `offset >= 0`, and `len > 0` in `CONSTRAINTS`; it separately requires `randomized[iv]` and ensures `preparedIV[this]`. These are declarative requirements, not an `if` condition in the source. `c1` does not bind `offset` or `len`, and the file does not explain how those constraints are handled for that event. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))
- **A name alone is not the match stated in the rule:** it identifies the governed class and the two parameter lists. Whether a particular analyzer could nevertheless match an unrelated method that merely shares the name cannot be determined from this rule file alone; it does not specify the analyzer’s matching implementation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

The file also does not define what establishes `randomized[iv]`, or observe the subsequent cipher mode or encryption/decryption operation. The URL points to a mutable branch; the supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified in this research pass. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/IvParameterSpec.crysl))

## Documented safe usage and remediation guidance

Oracle’s security guide says an IV should be random and need not necessarily be secret. `SecureRandom.nextBytes` is the documented API for obtaining random bytes. The applicable IV length and other requirements depend on the algorithm and mode. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/security-developer-guide.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/security-developer-guide.pdf and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html

For GCM specifically, Oracle requires IV uniqueness for encryption under a given key and directs callers to reinitialize with a different IV for each encryption. GCM also needs parameters beyond an IV, including the authentication-tag length. These are mode-specific requirements, not checks performed by `IvParameterSpec`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html))  
Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec.html

Oracle also documents allowing a provider to supply parameters when initializing for encryption, then retrieving them. This is not an unconditional guarantee of a random IV: the guide allows provider-specific defaults as well as generated random parameters. **For decryption, the same parameters used for encryption are required**, not a newly generated IV. The API documentation does not prescribe a finding-specific remediation when the detector details are unknown. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html

The cited OpenJDK implementation permits a zero-length selected range when its bounds are valid, whereas the CrySL rule declares `len > 0`. That constructor-level observation does not establish that a zero-length IV is valid for a particular cipher. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openjdk/jdk/master/src/java.base/share/classes/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.java))  
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openjdk/jdk/master/src/java.base/share/classes/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.java

## Compatibility and migration limits

- Oracle documents retrieving generated parameters through `Cipher.getParameters()` or `getIV()` and using the encryption parameters for decryption. Its guide illustrates saving an encoded `AlgorithmParameters` value; `SealedObject` attaches parameters to its encrypted contents. It does **not** specify a universal persisted or wire format for changing an existing application’s IV handling, nor a migration path for an unspecified existing format. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html))
- `IvParameterSpec` is documented since Java 1.4 and Android API level 1. The separate `GCMParameterSpec` is documented since Java 1.7 and Android API level 19. Class availability alone does not establish support for a particular cipher transformation or provider on a target platform. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec.html))  
  Sources: https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec and https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec
- The existing data format, protocol, provider, platform targets, and reported call are not supplied. Compatibility for a concrete change therefore remains unresolved.
